uncited: This family encompasses methods for generating the scalar or vector fields required for volume rendering, solving the problem of how to obtain or construct the input data structure (voxel grids, implicit fields, or simulation states) from continuous geometry, physical laws, or mathematical definitions.

It is distinguished from [Image-order rendering](16-image-order-rendering.md) and [Object-order rendering](22-object-order-rendering.md) by focusing on data creation rather than pixel projection, and from [Acquisition](14-acquisition.md) by including computational synthesis rather than just physical sensing.
All methods in this family map a conceptual or physical source into a discrete or analytic volumetric representation suitable for rendering.
**Domain Definition**: Establishing a spatial domain, typically a 3D grid with resolution $(N_x, N_y, N_z)$ and bounding box, or an infinite analytic space [S1, S3, unofficial].

**Value Assignment**: Determining the value (density, distance, color) for each point in the domain based on the source method (geometric intersection, function evaluation, or physical state) [S1, S12].
**Storage/Access**: Either storing the result in a discrete array (voxelization, simulation) or providing an interface to compute it on-the-fly (procedural) [S1, S3, unofficial].
The generation of volume data is fundamental to computer graphics and scientific visualization.
Early methods focused on voxelization of polygonal models for solid modeling and ray casting [S1].
Procedural volumes were popularized by Ken Perlin's noise functions and fractal Brownian motion in the 1980s for generating natural textures [S5, S6].
Simulation-based volumes emerged with the work of Jos Stam and others on stable fluids, enabling real-time rendering of dynamic phenomena [S1, S2].
Acquisition techniques have evolved from medical imaging (CT/MRI) to modern light field and volumetric video capture [S1, S3, unofficial].
